## CAV2-D67: Product Capability

Status: active
Term: product capability
Aliases: governed product capability, product behavior capability
Promoted: 2026-08-30 by explicit owner direction to make Capability Ontology canonical; definition authority only

### Normative Definition

A Product Capability is a stable, owner-qualified statement of an outcome that
one Product must enable for named participants or consumers while preserving
explicit scope, contracts, context policies, evidence routes, and authority
limits. It states what the Product must make possible and why that behavior
belongs to the Product. It does not select the agent, component, command,
interface, workflow, or implementation that realizes the outcome.

Every Product Capability belongs to exactly one Product. Its identity remains
stable while realizations, interfaces, evidence, and implementation technology
change, provided the outcome, Product anchor, scope, and owner boundary remain
the same. A material change to any of those anchors requires a successor
Product Capability rather than a silent rewrite.

### Formal Interpretation

```text
ProductCapability =
  (id, product_ref, outcome, scope, exclusions, participant_refs,
   consumer_refs, input_contract_refs, output_contract_refs,
   context_policy_refs, owner_routes, lifecycle_posture,
   realization_refs, evidence_refs, revision_history,
   challenge_route, authority_effect)

|product_ref| = 1
|owner_routes| >= 1
|consumer_refs| >= 1

lifecycle_posture =
  (kind, status, status_vocabulary_ref, evidence, commitment,
   provenance, owner, residue_refs)

lifecycle_posture.kind = product-capability
status_vocabulary_ref != null

valid(c) only if
  stable(c.id)
  and bounded(c.outcome, c.scope, c.exclusions)
  and contracts_resolve(c.input_contract_refs, c.output_contract_refs)
  and context_policies_resolve(c.context_policy_refs)
  and c.authority_effect = none

material_change(product_ref, outcome, scope, owner_routes) =>
  successor_product_capability_required

adopted(c) =/=> realized(c)
realized(c) =/=> conformant(c)
conformant(c) =/=> valuable(c)
observed(c) =/=> adopted(c)
permission_for(c) =/=> product_capability(c)
```

`lifecycle_posture` applies the `CAV2-D23` axis split. `status` is meaningful
only with its owning `status_vocabulary_ref`; this definition does not impose
one lifecycle enum on every capability. Evidence, owner commitment,
provenance, and residue remain separate posture fields. Realization,
conformance, and operational availability are separate axes owned by their
respective artifacts and evidence. None may be inferred from another or
collapsed into one `status` field.

### Schema

Schema handle: `CAV2-D67-SCHEMA` — tracked in
[DEFINITION-SCHEMAS.md](DEFINITION-SCHEMAS.md). Status: tracked (documentary).
The first closed machine-checkable candidate contract and business-system
bridge are owned by
[../../capability/schemas/capability.schema.json](../../capability/schemas/capability.schema.json).
The package references this definition and public `DEF-ARC-CAPABILITY`; it does
not replace either definition authority.

### Operational Interpretation

Define a Product Capability after the Product Thesis identifies an outcome the
Product must repeatedly enable. Name its consumers, scope, inputs, outputs,
context policies, owners, and exclusions before selecting a realization.
Later, bridge it to one or more Agent Capabilities or system realizations and
test that bridge with separate conformance and runtime evidence.

Keep capability instances with the module that owns their local meaning and
lifecycle. A central Capability Ontology may index or project those instances,
but it must not copy their authority or turn one registry into their owner.

### Plain-Language Intuition

A Product Capability says what useful thing the product must make possible. It
does not yet say which tool or implementation will do it.

### Domain-Context Voice

Inside CyberAlchemy v2, Define Shared Meaning, Resolve Bounded Language
Context, Resolve Registry Context, Governed Work Loop, and Governance
Enforcement are Product Capability candidates or projections owned by their
respective product and module surfaces. Public Arcanum Agent Capabilities such
as Invoke Define may realize part of a Product Capability, but the public
agent contract and the private product meaning remain separate authorities.

### Boundary

A Product Capability is not the Product, Product Thesis, Project (`CAV2-D60`),
Goal (`CAV2-D59`), Context (`CAV2-D66`), Agent Capability
(`DEF-ARC-CAPABILITY`), Bounded Context, business rule, implementation,
component, command, interface, workflow, service, permission, role, authority
grant, runtime process, test, metric, evidence receipt, or release state.

An adopted Product Capability is not proof of implementation. An implemented
realization is not proof of conformance. A passing conformance check is not
proof of customer value, product-market fit, authority transfer, publication,
release, deployment, or permission to execute.

## CAV2-D68: Person

Status: active
Term: person
Aliases: human individual
Promoted: 2026-08-31 by explicit owner direction to make Person a first-class CyberAlchemy v2 concept; definition authority only

### Normative Definition

A Person is one human individual whose identity may be referenced by
CyberAlchemy products, Projects, Contexts, Teams, responsibilities, decisions,
and evidence without reducing that human to an account, role, permission,
session, or machine-readable record.

Person identity remains distinct from every participation relationship. A
Person may join or leave Teams, hold different roles, own different work, use
multiple accounts, or have no digital account while remaining the same Person.
Any stored record is a bounded reference or projection of the Person, not the
Person itself. CyberAlchemy must minimize personal data and must not infer
private attributes merely because a Person is referenced.

### Formal Interpretation

```text
Person(p) => HumanIndividual(p)

represents(account, p) =/=> account = p
holds(p, role) =/=> p = role
member_of(p, team) requires exists membership
owns(p, artifact_or_decision) =/=> authorized_for(p, action)
observed(record_about_p) =/=> record_about_p = p

change(team_memberships(p), roles(p), accounts(p))
  =/=> successor_person_identity_required
```

Here `p` is a human individual. `represents`, `holds`, `member_of`, and `owns`
are relationships whose records and lifecycle remain independently owned. The
non-implications prevent identity, participation, ownership, and authority from
collapsing into one another.

### Operational Interpretation

Use Person when CyberAlchemy must refer to the same human across a Product,
Project, Goal, Context, Team, decision, or handoff. Keep accounts, interface
identities, memberships, roles, responsibilities, owner routes, and authority
grants as separate records linked to the Person reference. Collect only the
minimum attributes required by the named use and preserve the applicable
privacy, correction, challenge, and retirement routes.

### Plain-Language Intuition

A Person is the human, not their login, job title, permission, or database row.

### Domain-Context Voice

Inside CyberAlchemy v2, a Person may be a Human Participant, Work Owner,
reviewer, researcher, or member of one or more Teams. Those are ways the Person
participates. They do not replace the Person's identity and do not silently
grant authority. The People and Teams product owns the first business model
that connects these meanings while keeping sensitive personal data outside the
initial ontology.

### Boundary

A Person is not a user account, authentication subject, credential, contact,
employee record, customer record, legal identity assertion, profile, role,
permission, authority envelope, owner route, agent, model, session, or Team.
This definition does not establish identity verification, employment status,
consent, access rights, organizational hierarchy, or a right to process
personal data. A reference to a Person creates no authority effect.

## CAV2-D69: Team

Status: active
Term: team
Aliases: purpose-bound team
Promoted: 2026-08-31 by explicit owner direction to make Team a first-class CyberAlchemy v2 concept; definition authority only

### Normative Definition

A Team is a durable, owner-qualified collective identity through which Persons
coordinate toward one declared purpose and scope. Its identity, lifecycle,
membership, roles, responsibilities, and authority relationships are explicit
and remain separate.

A Team is not merely the current set of its members. Membership changes do not
silently create a different Team while its identity, purpose, scope, and owner
boundary remain stable. An active Team has at least one current Person
membership. A proposed Team may exist before its first membership so its
purpose and owner can be reviewed without inventing members.

### Formal Interpretation

```text
Team(t) => CollectiveIdentity(t)
purpose(t) != empty
owner_route(t) != empty

active(t) => exists p, m:
  Person(p)
  and TeamMembership(m)
  and binds(m, p, t)
  and current(m)

members(t, time_1) != members(t, time_2) =/=> t_at_time_1 != t_at_time_2
holds(team_or_person, role) =/=> authorized_for(team_or_person, action)
owns_responsibility(team_or_person, r) =/=> authority_grant(r)
```

Here `t` is the Team identity, `p` is a Person, and `m` is an independently
lifecycle-managed membership relation. Team membership, role assignment,
responsibility ownership, and authority are related but non-equivalent facts.

### Operational Interpretation

Create a Team with a stable identity, purpose, scope, owner route, lifecycle
state, and challenge route. Add Persons through explicit Team Membership
records. Attach Team Roles and Responsibilities through separately owned
assignments so that membership alone never implies a role, responsibility, or
permission. Preserve membership history rather than rewriting the current
member list as if earlier participation never existed.

### Plain-Language Intuition

A Team is a named group working toward a purpose. The group stays recognizable
even when its members change.

### Domain-Context Voice

Inside CyberAlchemy v2, a Team can coordinate Projects, Goals, definitions,
research, reviews, or product responsibilities. A Team may be named as an owner
route only when the corresponding ownership record says so. Team membership
alone does not make every member an owner or decision authority. The People and
Teams product owns the first candidate business ontology for these relations.

### Boundary

A Team is not a Product, Project, Goal, organization, company, department,
mailing list, chat channel, access group, permission group, role, owner route,

# Arcanum Canonical Definitions

Status: active
Owner: definitions-governance
Canonical source: `definitions/DEFINITIONS.md`
Lookup index: `definitions/DEFINITIONS-INDEX.md`

## Authority Rule

Only this file defines normative semantics for Arcanum-wide terms it contains.
Downstream artifacts may explain, apply, or reference these terms, but should
not redefine them as global authority.

Feature glossaries, refinement-run glossaries, work-pack glossaries, and
capability-local vocabulary may define local terms. Promote those terms here
only when they are intended to become Arcanum-wide vocabulary.

## DEF-ARC-CONTRACT: Contract

Status: active
Term: contract
Aliases: output contract, mode contract, handoff contract, execution contract,
artifact contract, source contract

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A contract is an explicit behavioral and authority agreement for an Arcanum
artifact, capability, route, stage, or handoff. It states what the thing
promises, who owns the result, what inputs, outputs, evidence, and boundaries
are required, and what conditions cause pass, flag, block, handoff, deferral,
or rejection.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a contract to decide whether behavior is allowed, whether an artifact
satisfies its obligation, which owner has authority, and when work must stop,
route elsewhere, or produce more evidence.

### Plain-Language Voice

A contract is the promise around the work: what it is allowed to mean, do,
require, and prove.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, contracts appear in sigil `SKILL.md` files, spell mode
contracts, dispatch routes, work-packs, task-session reports, and handoff
artifacts. They are the operating boundary used by Arcanum agents to decide
whether a route may proceed, must block, should defer, or should hand off to a
different owner. The reader-facing `development/user-guide/` material may
explain contracts as part of the Arcanum development loop, but this definition
remains the authority for the Arcanum-wide term.

### Boundary

A contract may reference a schema, but it is not only field shape. A route,
stage, or artifact does not satisfy its contract merely because a schema
validates; it must also meet the behavioral, ownership, evidence, and boundary
conditions named by the contract.

### Primary Consumers

- `README.md`
- `registry/`
- `framework/`
- `formulae/dispatch-spec/`
- `spells/`
- `arcana/task-session/`
- `arcana/refine/`
- `transmutations/context-builder/`
- `development/craft/`

### Related Definitions

- `DEF-ARC-SCHEMA`

## DEF-ARC-SCHEMA: Schema

Status: active
Term: schema
Aliases: dispatch schema, ledger schema, artifact schema, row-family schema,
YAML schema, JSON Schema

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A schema is an explicit structural representation of valid artifact, data,
route, ledger, or runtime state. It defines fields, row families, types,
enums, references, cardinality, shape constraints, and parse or validation
rules used to store, exchange, inspect, or validate instances.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a schema to check whether an instance has the required structure. Pair it
with a contract to decide what that structure means, who owns it, and whether
it proves the required behavior.

### Plain-Language Voice

A schema is the form the evidence must fit.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, schemas appear in dispatch validation, Craft ledgers,
artifact metadata, definition indexes, and generated or runtime-facing
structured files. They give agents a parseable shape to inspect before a
contract decides what that shape means. The Arcanum user-guide can use schemas
as examples of governed structure, but schema validity is not by itself
execution proof, promotion proof, or authority transfer.

### Boundary

Schema validation is shape evidence, not execution evidence, promotion
evidence, or authority transfer by itself. A schema can support a contract, but
it does not replace the contract's behavioral and ownership claims.

### Primary Consumers

- `framework/SCHEMA-CONSTITUTION.md`
- `formulae/dispatch-spec/`
- `development/craft/`
- `benchmark/`
- validation scripts and fixtures

### Related Definitions

- `DEF-ARC-CONTRACT`

## DEF-ARC-GOAL-SPELL: Goal Spell

Status: active
Term: goal spell
Aliases: autonomous goal loop, goal loop, DAG goal loop

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A goal spell is an Arcanum spell that routes a bounded goal over a governed work
graph through frontier reading, risk classification, owner and technique
selection, delegated execution, audit, staged-delta proposal, and
approval-gated promotion.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a goal spell when a goal should advance through existing Arcanum
capabilities while preserving owner boundaries, stop conditions, reviewable
evidence, staged source changes, and explicit approval before protected
mutation.

### Plain-Language Voice

A goal spell is the conductor for a goal: it decides what can run, who should
do it, when to stop, and what must be approved before source truth changes.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, `spells/goal/` is the draft reusable goal spell. Its local
source contract, spec, and package glossary explain goal-specific phases and
handoff artifacts, while this definition provides the Arcanum-wide meaning for
the term.

### Boundary

A goal spell is not a replacement for delegated sigils or spells. It routes to
owners and records evidence; it does not redefine the internal contracts of
`craft`, `dispatch-spec`, `decision-gate`, `task-session`, observability
capabilities, or other delegated owners.

### Primary Consumers

- `spells/goal/`
- `arcana/task-session/`
- `arcana/craft/`
- `formulae/dispatch-spec/`
- `spells/observed-invocation-loop/`
- `arcana/decision-gate/`
- `formulae/observability-setup/`

### Related Definitions

- `DEF-ARC-APPROVAL-TOKEN`

## DEF-ARC-STAGED-DELTA: Staged Delta

Status: active
Term: staged delta
Aliases: proposed delta, staged proposal, proposed ledger delta

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A staged delta is a proposed change to an authoritative source that records the
target, operation, framed diff or equivalent review surface, validation
expectation, and promotion state before any active source-of-truth mutation is
applied.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a staged delta when a capability has evidence for a source change but the
change requires review, approval, validation, or batching before it can mutate
the authoritative artifact.

### Plain-Language Voice

A staged delta is a held change: visible, reviewable, and not yet applied.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, staged deltas are used by the draft `spells/goal/` contract
to keep Craft ledger changes proposal-only until approval. Other Arcanum
capabilities may use the same term when they separate proposal evidence from
active mutation.

### Boundary

A staged delta is not proof that the change is correct or approved. It is review
state. Application still depends on the relevant contract, validation surface,
and approval policy.

### Primary Consumers

- `spells/goal/`
- `arcana/craft/`
- `arcana/task-session/`
- `arcana/decision-gate/`

### Related Definitions

- `DEF-ARC-CONTRACT`
- `DEF-ARC-APPROVAL-TOKEN`

## DEF-ARC-APPROVAL-TOKEN: Approval Token

Status: active
Term: approval token
Aliases: apply token, batch approval token, promotion token

### Scientific/Formal Voice

An approval token is an explicit authorization artifact that binds an approver,
a reviewed batch or operation, a decision record or equivalent durable approval
reference, and an approval state before a protected mutation may execute.

### Operational Interpretation

Use an approval token to decide whether a protected operation may move from
proposal to application. The token should identify exactly what is approved and
which durable record or evidence supports that approval.

### Plain-Language Voice

An approval token is the clear yes for this exact batch that lets a protected
change move from proposal to apply.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, the draft `spells/goal/` contract uses approval tokens for
batch promotion of staged deltas. Decision Gate supplies durable decision
evidence; Craft or another owner applies the approved change according to its
own contract.

### Boundary

An approval token should not be ambient authority. It applies to the named
batch or operation only, and it does not authorize unrelated source mutation,
publication, commits, pushes, parent gitlink movement, or promotion unless those
operations are explicitly included.

### Primary Consumers

- `spells/goal/`
- `arcana/decision-gate/`
- `arcana/craft/`
- `arcana/task-session/`

### Related Definitions

- `DEF-ARC-CONTRACT`
- `DEF-ARC-STAGED-DELTA`

## DEF-ARC-DEVELOPMENT-ARTIFACT: Development Artifact

Status: active
Term: development artifact
Aliases: run artifact, candidate artifact, development package, refinement
artifact, invoke artifact, task-session artifact

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A development artifact is a non-authoritative artifact produced during
exploration, refinement, design, planning, validation, task execution, runtime
observation, or maintenance. It may carry evidence, candidate wording, proposed
structure, validation results, or promotion recommendations, but it does not
define canonical Arcanum behavior, terminology, architecture, registry state, or
artifact policy until an owning promotion route applies a reviewed change to the
target canonical artifact.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a development artifact as source evidence or a proposal input. Before using
its content to change a canonical artifact, resolve the target owner, extract
the smallest durable claim, frame the change as a staged delta or promotion
patch, and run the target artifact's validation and approval gates.

### Plain-Language Voice

A development artifact is working evidence. It can suggest what source truth
should become, but it is not source truth by itself.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, development artifacts commonly live under
`<tier>/<canonical-id>/development/`, `spells/<canonical-id>/development/`,
`development/refinement-runs/`, `development/task-sessions/`, or related
runtime evidence folders. An architecture development artifact can propose an
architecture rule, but the rule becomes authoritative only after it is patched
into the canonical architecture artifact through the owning route.

### Boundary

A development artifact should not be cited as canonical authority just because
it is detailed, validated for its own run, or generated by a trusted capability.
It may remain useful evidence even when the promotion route rejects or narrows
the proposed canonical change.

### Primary Consumers

- `framework/ARTIFACT-CONSTITUTION.md`
- `framework/DEVELOPMENT-TO-CANONICAL-PROMOTION.md`
- `arcana/architecture-pattern-inventory/`
- `arcana/task-session/`
- `arcana/refine/`
- `spells/invoke/`

## DEF-ARC-CANONICAL-ARTIFACT: Canonical Artifact

Status: active
Term: canonical artifact
Aliases: source artifact, source-of-truth artifact, authoritative artifact,
canonical source, promoted artifact

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A canonical artifact is a versioned Arcanum source artifact whose owning
contract gives it authority to define reusable behavior, terminology, process,
architecture, templates, schemas, registry state, validation policy, or other
durable repository semantics for its declared scope.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a canonical artifact to decide the current authoritative rule for its scope.
Mutate it only through the owner route named by its artifact type, adjacent
contract, framework policy, or registry/lifecycle rule. When development
evidence conflicts with a canonical artifact, treat the evidence as a promotion
candidate or drift finding until the canonical artifact is explicitly patched.

### Plain-Language Voice

A canonical artifact is the place the repository agrees to treat as source
truth for a specific kind of work.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, canonical artifacts include files under `arcana/`,
`spells/`, `transmutations/`, `framework/`, `definitions/`, `disciplines/`,
`registry/`, and `tools/` when those files define reusable Arcanum behavior or
policy. Canonical architecture artifacts may be package-level architecture docs,
architecture inventory outputs, or framework architecture standards, depending
on the owner and declared scope.

### Boundary

A canonical artifact is authoritative only for the scope it declares. It does
not inherit unrelated authority from adjacent development folders, generated
runtime surfaces, validation logs, or narrative summaries.

### Primary Consumers

## DEF-ARC-PROMOTION-PATCH: Promotion Patch

Status: active
Term: promotion patch
Aliases: canonicalization patch, development-to-canonical patch, promotion
delta, canonical patch

### Scientific/Formal Voice

A promotion patch is a reviewed mutation to a canonical artifact that derives
from one or more development artifacts or other evidence sources and records
the target canonical artifact, source evidence, owner route, selected durable
claim or structure, transformation rationale, validation expectation, and
approval or rejection state.

### Operational Interpretation

Use a promotion patch when working content should move from development evidence
into canonical source. The patch should normalize the content into the target
artifact's voice and contract, cite the source evidence, update required lookup
or generated surfaces, run validation, and leave rejected or deferred material
behind as development evidence rather than silently carrying it into authority.

### Plain-Language Voice

A promotion patch is the careful move from "this looks right in development" to
"this is now the source rule."

### Domain Context

In this workspace, promotion patches are the process for cases such as applying
architecture development artifact content to a canonical architecture artifact,
promoting a local glossary term into `definitions/DEFINITIONS.md`, or moving a
validated capability change from `development/` into a `SKILL.md`, README,
framework constitution, or registry row.

### Boundary

A promotion patch is not a bulk copy, a commit by itself, or proof that all
source evidence is now canonical. It must name what was selected, what stayed
candidate, which owner accepted the mutation, and which validation passed or
remains blocking.

## DEF-ARC-CAPABILITY: Agent Capability

Status: active
Term: agent capability
Aliases: reusable agent capability, governed agent capability

### Scientific/Formal Voice

An Agent Capability is a stable, owner-qualified promise that an agent system
can perform one reusable kind of work under explicit applicability, input,
output, failure, evidence, and authority boundaries. The capability is the
meaningful behavior contract, not any single prompt, model call, run, process,
installation, or interface that realizes it.

```text
AgentCapability =
  (id, purpose, applicability, exclusions, input_contract_refs,
   behavior_contract_ref, output_contract_refs, quality_conditions,
   failure_contract, owner_route, observability_refs,
   lifecycle_owner_route, revision_history, challenge_route)

valid(c) only if
  stable(c.id)
  and bounded(c.purpose, c.applicability, c.exclusions)
  and owned(c.owner_route)
  and explicit(c.failure_contract)
  and owned(c.lifecycle_owner_route)
  and contracts_resolve(c.input_contract_refs,
                        c.behavior_contract_ref,
                        c.output_contract_refs)

run(c) =/=> c
prompt_for(c) =/=> c
installed(c) =/=> validated(c)
observed(c) =/=> authority(c)
```

`id` preserves identity across individual runs. `purpose`, `applicability`, and
`exclusions` say what reusable work the capability does and when it does not
apply. The contract references define admitted inputs, outputs, and behavior;
`quality_conditions` say what useful execution must preserve. `owner_route`
controls contract change. `failure_contract` states when the capability flags,
blocks, defers, or hands off. `lifecycle_owner_route` names the authority that
owns the capability's lifecycle vocabulary and transitions; this definition
does not impose one lifecycle enum on every Arcanum capability.
`observability_refs` and `revision_history` support improvement without
pretending that observations rewrite the contract. `challenge_route` keeps
disagreement explicit.

### Operational Interpretation

Use an Agent Capability when a recurring unit of agent work needs a stable name
and contract that can survive changes to prompts, models, host adapters, and
individual executions. Compose capabilities by referencing their contracts;
route a contract change back to the capability owner.

### Plain-Language Voice

An Agent Capability is a named job an agent can do again, with clear inputs,
outputs, limits, failure behavior, and an owner.

### Domain Context

In this workspace, sigils package reusable Agent Capabilities and spells
compose them into larger routes. Invoke Define is one capability-bearing mode:
its files, schemas, validators, and host adapters may change while its owned
behavioral promise remains separately identifiable. Observation and reflection
may justify a later revision, but they do not silently change that promise.

### Boundary

An Agent Capability is not a Product Capability, prompt, model, agent persona,
skill installation, command, interface, runtime process, session, individual
run, evidence receipt, permission, authority grant, sigil file, or spell graph.
A sigil may package one Agent Capability and a spell may compose capabilities;
neither relationship makes packaging, composition, installation, or execution
equivalent to the capability's meaning. Passing one run does not make the
capability validated, active, adopted by a product, or authorized for every
context.

## DomainSpec Definitions (wedge)

> Canonical, machine-checkable definitions of the **DomainSpec** domain-modeling
> vocabulary — the open-core methodology surface. The formal `DS-*` IDs below are
> the source of truth; `TAXONOMY.md` and `RELATIONSHIPS.md` are the prose example
> layer that points here.
>
> **Term boundary:** the DomainSpec meta-type and edge vocabulary (Entity, Mapping,
> Adapter, `contracts` edge, …) is domain-modeling vocabulary and is distinct from the
> Arcanum-native governance terms `DEF-ARC-CONTRACT` / `DEF-ARC-SCHEMA` above. Where a
> word coincides (e.g. the `contracts` relationship verb), the DomainSpec meaning is the
> typed graph-edge, not the Arcanum authority agreement.

### DS-D1: Meta-Type System

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Let:

$$
\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{M}_B \cup \mathcal{M}_U
$$

Canonical composition-extension profile (25 backend types):

$$
\mathcal{M}_B = \{Entity, ValueObject, Enum, Operation, Query, Calculation, Rule, Policy, Workflow, Interface, Event, Mapping, StateMachine, Saga\}
$$

$$
\mathcal{M}_U = \{Page, Layout, Component, ViewModel, Hook, Form, Action, Guard, Binding, Adapter, StateIndicator\}
$$

(A 24-type pre-composition baseline — `\mathcal{M}_B` without `Saga` — exists historically; the canonical profile is the 25-type set above. Report profile-specific counts explicitly in evidence.)

#### Plain-Language Voice

This is the allowed concept-type vocabulary. Profile-specific counts keep
baseline and extended semantics from being mixed in evidence reports.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-D1 types are used by DomainSpec concept registries,
`definitions/TAXONOMY.md`, and definitions-governance concept-registry
aggregation. Feature-local concepts should use these meta-types for typed
analysis, but new local vocabulary remains package-local until
definitions-governance promotes it.

### DS-D2: Typed Relationship System

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Let:

$$
\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}_B \cup \mathcal{R}_U \cup \mathcal{R}_X
$$

$$
\mathcal{R}_B = \{performs, produces, enforces, calculates, transitions, exposes, orchestrates, applies, maps, contains, queries, emits\}
$$

$$
\mathcal{R}_U = \{renders, wraps, composes, consumes, submits, shapes, protects, displays\}
$$

$$
\mathcal{R}_X = \{fetches, mutates, reflects, derives, contracts, mirrors\}
$$

Canonical composition-extension profile (29 edges) adds cross-feature relations:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{CF} = \{produces\text{-}for, triggers\text{-}cross, enforces\text{-}cross\}
$$

$$
\mathcal{R}^{29} = \mathcal{R}_B \cup \mathcal{R}_U \cup \mathcal{R}_X \cup \mathcal{R}_{CF}
$$

#### Plain-Language Voice

This is the allowed relationship-verb vocabulary, grouped by backend, UI, and
cross-layer role, with optional cross-feature relations for composition-heavy
analyses.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-D2 relation verbs are explained by
`definitions/RELATIONSHIPS.md` and used by DomainSpec concept graphs, registry
aggregation, and integration-style analysis. The `contracts` relationship verb
is a DomainSpec typed edge and is distinct from `DEF-ARC-CONTRACT`.

**Canon boundary.** The canonical vocabulary is exactly the 25-type / 29-edge composition-extension profile above, as shipped in `TAXONOMY.md` and `RELATIONSHIPS.md`. No larger edge or category extension is adopted; any such proposal is deferred design rationale, not canonical vocabulary.

### DS-D3: Concept Graph

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

A feature-level concept graph is:

$$
G = (V, E, \tau, \lambda)
$$

where $V$ is concept vertices, $E \subseteq V \times V$ is directed edges, $\tau: V \rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ is meta-type assignment, and $\lambda: E \rightarrow \mathcal{R}$ is edge-type assignment.

#### Plain-Language Voice

A feature is modeled as a typed graph: nodes are concepts, edges are
relationships, and both carry explicit semantics.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, concept graphs are the bridge between feature-level
DomainSpec artifacts and higher-level governance checks. They let agents audit
whether a feature's concepts and relationships follow DS-D1 and DS-D2 before
those concepts are reused by inventories, integration specs, or downstream
planning.

### DS-D7: Edge-Family Partition

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Relationship families are disjoint:

$$
\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}_B \uplus \mathcal{R}_U \uplus \mathcal{R}_X
$$

and in composition-enabled analyses may extend to $\mathcal{R}^{+} = \mathcal{R} \uplus \mathcal{R}_{CF}$.

#### Plain-Language Voice

Each edge family has one semantic home. Optional cross-feature edges are
explicit extensions, not hidden overloads of the base vocabulary.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, edge-family partitioning prevents backend, UI, cross-layer,
and cross-feature relationship meanings from collapsing into one ambiguous
edge list. It is used when DomainSpec examples, relationship catalogs, and
concept-registry aggregation need to explain why an edge belongs to one family
rather than another.

### DS-D8: Edge-Signature Operator

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Let $\sigma: \mathcal{R} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}) \times \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})$. A typed edge instance $e=(u,r,v)$ is valid iff:

$$
\tau(u) \in \pi_1(\sigma(r)) \land \tau(v) \in \pi_2(\sigma(r))
$$

#### Plain-Language Voice

Relation typing behaves like a graph type-checker: the source and target
concept types must fit the declared signature for the selected relationship.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-D8 is the validation rule behind concept-graph and
concept-registry edge checks. It is the reason definitions-governance
aggregation should reject an edge whose endpoint meta-types do not match the
declared DomainSpec relationship signature.

### DS-D10: Coverage-Status Taxonomy

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Concept mapping status: `covered`, `strained`, `uncovered`. Edge modeling status: `works`, `strained`, `broken`. Cross-experiment synthesis must preserve these vocabularies without relabeling.

#### Plain-Language Voice

Fixed status vocabularies keep evidence comparable across experiments and
reruns.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-D10 status labels are used when DomainSpec coverage
experiments, concept mapping, and edge modeling need comparable evidence. They
help later reviewers distinguish a missing concept, a strained mapping, and a
broken relationship without inventing new status words in every report.

### DS-P1: Type Safety Property

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

All edge instances satisfy signature constraints (no relation may connect concept types that violate the declared signature).

#### Plain-Language Voice

No relationship may connect two concept types that its declared signature does
not allow.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-P1 is the acceptance property for DomainSpec typed
graphs and concept-registry aggregation. A feature graph that violates DS-P1
should be flagged before its relationships are reused as planning or
integration evidence.

### DS-P2: Backend/UI Partition Property

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

$\mathcal{M}_B \cap \mathcal{M}_U = \emptyset$ for the selected profile. Backend and UI type sets are intentionally non-overlapping to reduce ambiguity.

#### Plain-Language Voice

Backend types and UI types are separate buckets. A concept should not count as
both under the same profile.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-P2 helps DomainSpec feature artifacts and audits keep
backend model terms separate from UI projection terms. That separation is what
lets later guides, inventories, and implementation plans talk about backend
behavior and UI behavior without silently merging their meanings.

### DS-P3: Cross-Layer Direction Property

#### Scientific/Formal Voice

Edges in $\mathcal{R}_X$ are directed UI → backend. Cross-layer interactions use a single directional semantics for consistency.

#### Plain-Language Voice

Cross-layer edges point from UI concepts toward the backend concepts they
fetch, mutate, reflect, derive from, contract with, or mirror.

#### Domain Context

In this workspace, DS-P3 keeps DomainSpec cross-layer analysis directional:
UI artifacts may depend on, reflect, or invoke backend concepts, but the edge
vocabulary should not imply that backend domain concepts are authored by UI
views. This protects guide, integration, and planning artifacts from reversing
ownership when they explain UI/backend relationships.

# Sigil: Complexity Example Ladder

<objective>
Turn one evidence-bounded explanation or comparison into aligned low-, medium-,
and complex examples that increase structural complexity without changing the
underlying concept, options, recommendation, or authority state.
</objective>

<logic-type>
Transmutation: bounded example synthesis and complexity calibration.
</logic-type>

<trigger>
Use this sigil when:

- the user asks to explain, illustrate, or provide examples,
- a caller contract requires complexity-calibrated examples,
- multiple options need comparable examples before a human choice,
- interacting identity, state, dependency, boundary, or failure conditions make
  an abstract distinction hard to evaluate.

Do not invoke it for unrelated factual or mechanical answers merely to add prose.
For Decision Gate, invoke only after the user selects "Explain / more context" or
otherwise signals uncertainty.
</trigger>

<inputs>
Resolve, when available:

- the subject, question, or decision being explained,
- authoritative source evidence and its claim ceiling,
- the invariant concept or distinction that must stay fixed across all rungs,
- every admissible action option when the mode is comparative,
- defer and stop choices when their continuation effects matter,
- constraints, assumptions, and authority boundaries,
- caller and trigger kind,
- audience baseline and optional complexity axes.

If the source cannot support a rung and a safe hypothetical cannot be labeled,
return `BLOCK` rather than fabricate the example.
</inputs>

<complexity-model>
- `low`: one primary concept or action; local context; no material dependency;
  reversible or consequence-light behavior.
- `medium`: multiple interacting concepts or options; at least one dependency,
  state change, boundary, or downstream consequence.
- `complex`: several actors, layers, states, or dependencies plus an exception,
  uncertainty, failure path, authority boundary, or dependent decision.

These are structural differences, not word-count, jargon, or detail targets.
</complexity-model>

<process>
1. Determine mode:
   - `explanatory` for one concept or mechanism,
   - `comparative` for two or more admissible options.
2. Separate source evidence, caller-provided constraints, and agent inference.
   Label every invented scenario detail as hypothetical.
3. Extract one invariant concept, distinction, or comparison that must remain
   stable across all three rungs.
4. Choose the smallest useful structural complexity axes from interacting
   concepts, dependencies, state, boundaries, consequences, exceptions, and
   uncertainty.
5. Build the low example. Keep it local and remove nonessential dependencies.
6. Build the medium example by preserving the low invariant and adding at least
   one interaction, dependency, state change, boundary, or consequence.
7. Build the complex example by preserving the same invariant and adding a
   cross-boundary interaction, exception, ambiguity, failure path, authority
   consequence, or dependent decision.
8. State explicitly what each rung adds over the previous rung.
9. In comparative mode:
   - reuse the same scenario for every admissible action option within a rung,
   - give every option equivalent explanatory depth,
   - show defer and stop only as unchanged or terminated continuation states,
   - do not change option wording, recommendation, or admissibility.
10. For each rung, state what it demonstrates and what it does not prove.
11. Validate that all three rungs exist, the invariant is preserved, option
    coverage is even, unsupported claims are zero, and decision effect is none.
12. Return the ladder. If called by a decision workflow, return control without
    selecting, recording, admitting, executing, or authorizing an option.
</process>

<observability>
A meaningful execution is an attempted or completed three-rung ladder.

When repository observability is available, record the standard sigil signal plus:

- trigger kind and caller,
- explanatory or comparative mode,
- required and produced rungs,
- complexity axes,
- invariant-preservation result,
- required options and per-rung coverage,
- hypothetical count,
- unsupported-claim count,
- unequal-option-coverage flag,
- decision effect,
- user correction signal.

Default reflection triggers are 5 meaningful executions, 10 generated outputs,
3 related gaps, or 1 severe gap. Severe gaps include unlabelled fabrication,
examples treated as consent or selection, material option bias, and private/public
or authority-boundary leakage.
</observability>

<quality-bar>
A successful execution must:

- produce low, medium, and complex rungs,
- increase structural complexity at every rung,
- preserve one stable concept or comparison invariant,
- distinguish evidence from labelled hypothetical details,
- use one shared scenario per rung in comparative mode,
- cover every admissible action option evenly,
- keep defer and stop as continuation states rather than invented product behavior,
- state what each example demonstrates and does not prove,
- report any unsupported claim instead of hiding it,
- preserve the caller's recommendation, admissibility, gate, and authority state,
- keep public templates and experiment fixtures product-neutral,
- return `decision effect: none` whenever a decision is involved.
</quality-bar>

<anti-patterns>
Avoid:

- increasing length without increasing structural complexity,
- changing the core subject or invariant between rungs,
- equating jargon with complexity,
- introducing unsupported domain facts,
- presenting a hypothetical as source evidence,
- giving a recommended option richer or more favorable examples,
- using unrelated scenarios that prevent controlled comparison,
- silently omitting a rung or admissible action option,
- turning an example into a recommendation, choice, consent, or owner approval,
- treating the ladder as application-specific validity or admissibility proof,
- expanding into implementation, mutation, promotion, publication, or execution,
- copying caller-private material into public sigil examples or fixtures.
</anti-patterns>

<output-contract>
Return:

```markdown
## Complexity Example Ladder Result

- Status: pass | block
- Subject: <subject or decision>
- Mode: explanatory | comparative
- Complexity basis: <structural axes>
- Evidence: <sources or supplied context>
- Assumptions: <labelled hypotheticals or none>

### Low
- Scenario: <shared low scenario>
- Example: <concept behavior or every option under the scenario>
- Demonstrates: <what becomes visible>
- Limits: <what this does not prove>

### Medium
- Added complexity: <structural addition>
- Scenario: <shared medium scenario>
- Example: <concept behavior or every option under the scenario>
- Demonstrates: <what becomes visible>
- Limits: <what this does not prove>

### Complex
- Added complexity: <structural addition>
- Scenario: <shared complex scenario>
- Example: <concept behavior or every option under the scenario>
- Demonstrates: <what becomes visible>
- Limits: <what this does not prove>

### Coverage
- Rungs produced: <n>/3
- Options covered: <IDs or not applicable>
- Unsupported claims: <count and details>
- Decision effect: none | not applicable
- Next step: <return to caller | supply missing evidence>
```
</output-contract>

# CyberAlchemy Define CLI

This package is the candidate conversational terminal realization of `CA2-CAP-DEFINE-SHARED-MEANING`.
It is ready for local testing, but it is not accepted, published, deployed, or installed globally.

The primary conversational command performs one bounded reviewed lifecycle:

```text
broad new-work / domain / subject / context / project opening
  -> persistent ARE gateway
  -> shared app-server RPC client
  -> conversational discovery through the Codex app-server wrapper
  -> direct user-language capture across terms, distinctions, relationships, constraints, ownership, and open questions
  -> explicit scope review and confirmation
  -> candidate meaning options
  -> one-option-at-a-time review
  -> verified ARE route and frozen inline Context Envelope
  -> candidate Definition Pack
  -> explicit Definition Pack Alch handoff
  -> generated semantic-contract ontology
  -> Craft / DomainSpec project and compilation
  -> candidate executable runtime projection plus digest-bound receipt
```

The agent may reflect, summarize, and propose. It preserves the user's phrases separately from
candidate interpretations and may not silently confirm its own inference. For unbounded new-work
intent, scope cannot become ready until the user has addressed the desired outcome, consumers,
terms, distinctions and relationships, constraints, ownership, and open questions. Unknown and
not-applicable answers remain valid user answers rather than being invented by the agent.

Before presenting scope for confirmation, the runtime evaluates a structured language-quality
contract. Every language item must point to an exact user phrase; every unordered term pair must
carry non-collapse evidence; and every declared classification-axis pair must be independent or
have an explicit typed coupling. Candidate inferences remain `review` until the user confirms
them. Missing grounding, collapsed terms, redundant axes, unresolved pairs, and unnamed coupling
block pack creation. These deterministic checks validate coverage and concrete contradictions;
they do not prove canonical semantic truth.
The exact scope requires a human confirmation, and every option requires an explicit accept,
edit, discuss, or defer action.

Define's semantic and workflow dispositions are no longer owned by handwritten
prototype code. Their canonical construction sources are the `.alch` files in
`alch/`, assembled by `alch/define-runtime.alch` as eleven non-overlapping entry
points. `GroundingEvidence`, `NonCollapseEvidence`, and
`OrthogonalityEvidence` own per-record posture meaning; `SemanticGrounding`,
`NonCollapse`, `Orthogonality`, and `LanguageReadiness` own quality aggregation;
`ScopeReadiness`, `ConceptDisposition`, and `PackReadiness` carry the pack
workflow decisions. `AlchHandoffReadiness` independently requires structural
readiness, semantic grounding, non-collapse, orthogonality, and a new output
target before compilation. The exact candidate business and system ontology records are selected in
`alch/define-runtime.ontology-selection.json`.

```text
host evidence extraction and interaction adapters
  -> canonical multi-entry AlchLang declarations
  -> source-linked composition ontology for every entry
  -> Craft / DomainSpec v2 project for every entry
  -> generated executable decision service
  -> conversational scope, disposition, and Definition Pack gates
```

JavaScript remains responsible for model/RPC transport, evidence collection,
user-facing prose, canonical object construction, context-source
reads, persistence, locks, atomic writes, and audit delivery. Those adapters
consume the generated decisions rather than independently replacing them.
The condition-by-condition boundary is recorded in
`HOST-SEMANTIC-INVENTORY.md`.

Unicode semantic-key normalization and boundary-aware phrase containment are
declared by the Alch semantic prelude and consumed through its shared direct
compiled-artifact adapter. Define, Router, and ARE request intent bind the same
runtime bytes while retaining separate quality, route, and objective policies.
The exact dependency and construction pipeline are recorded in
`alch/define-runtime.ontology-selection.json`; the host no longer implements
those two semantics itself.

`npm test` runs `scripts/verify-alch-runtime.mjs` first. Verification blocks on
a missing `.alch` source, selected-ontology drift, service-entry drift,
ontology or Craft-project mismatch, compiler-certificate mismatch,
generated-file drift, incorrect executable outcomes, or non-repeatable
recompilation. Generated output remains candidate construction evidence and
grants no ontology admission or runtime authority.

## Definition Pack Alch handoff

A reviewed, handoff-ready conversational result can be materialized explicitly:

```bash
$NODE cyberAlchemy-v2/implementation/define-cli/bin/define.mjs compile \
  --input /path/to/definition-pack-result.json \
  --out /path/to/new-definition-contract
```

The output directory must not exist. It contains `definition-pack.alch`, finite
language fixtures, `compiled/`, and `handoff-receipt.json`. The compiler pipeline
is recorded as Definition Pack, Alch source, semantic-contract ontology, Craft
project, DomainSpec compilation, runtime projection, and fixture validation.
The receipt binds the exact pack, source, fixture, and compiler manifest digests.

Compilation blocks if the pack has open meaning, lacks a reviewed language-quality
evaluation, or if semantic grounding, non-collapse, or orthogonality does not
pass. This is a candidate semantic runtime projection, not generated product
behavior: it does not make the definitions canonical and does not authorize
implementation, effects, publication, or deployment.

## Durable session runtime

The package also exports a transport-neutral durable session core for CLI and
chat adapters. It implements the smallest unit selected by the Define runtime
design: one versioned command against one expected revision, followed by one
atomic confirmed-state boundary.

`createDurableDefineRuntime`, `createDefineSessionClient`, and
`JsonFileSessionRepository` provide:

- complete resumable snapshots with exact state digests;
- shared CLI/chat session identity without interface-owned state;
- optimistic revision conflicts and command-id idempotency;
- atomic mode-0600 JSON persistence and tamper detection;
- visible denied, invalid, conflict, incompatible-schema, and storage-failure
  outcomes; and
- content-minimizing audit records that exclude prompts, answers, sources, and
  raw session identifiers.

`resolveDefineContextCandidates` applies the committed explicit-user,
related-reference, current-window, and saved-session order without allowing an
inferred candidate to overwrite explicit context. Conflicts and the need for
user correction remain visible. `createDefineContextSufficiencyAdapter` maps
the private semantic-judgment evaluator into the Define three-valued result and
caches exact frozen requests so historical replay does not rerun evaluation.

The in-memory repository remains available for deterministic tests. The file
repository is a local candidate backend, not an adopted storage, backup,
retention, encryption, or deployment choice. Actor access context must be
supplied by a trusted adapter; this package does not invent an identity
provider.

## Conversational run

Use the repository-supported Node binary:

```bash
NODE=/home/vrondelli/.nvm/versions/node/v26.8.1/bin/node
$NODE cyberAlchemy-v2/implementation/define-cli/bin/define.mjs
```

You can also supply the broad opening immediately:

```bash
$NODE cyberAlchemy-v2/implementation/define-cli/bin/define.mjs \
  "We are building a knowledge system for clinical research teams and the language is becoming inconsistent"
```

The conversational path connects to the persistent ARE gateway at
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/are-codex/gateway.sock` (or `/run/user/<uid>/are-codex/gateway.sock`) and
creates an ephemeral read-only Codex thread on the `codex:human-chat` interaction lane. The
gateway preserves its consumer runtime across transport reconnects; Define itself does not
create durable conversation storage. Use `--gateway-socket <path>` for a different gateway.

`--direct` is an explicit diagnostic fallback that spawns the strict app-server wrapper for
this process. It does not permit protocol drift and is not the normal conversational path.
Use `--output <path>` to atomically retain the final pack, and `--json` to print the complete
result instead of the compact human summary.

## Advanced scripted run

`define run` retains the deterministic exact-input interface for automation:

```bash
$NODE cyberAlchemy-v2/implementation/define-cli/bin/define.mjs run \
  --goal "Define a release channel" \
  --intent "Remove ambiguity for a local consumer" \
  --context "A release channel names how candidate output reaches a consumer." \
  --consumer local-test \
  --input cyberAlchemy-v2/implementation/define-cli/fixtures/smoke-input.json \
  --json
```

Scripted input has this shape:

```json
{
  "concepts": [{"concept_id":"concept:term","term":"term","question":"What does term mean?","owner_route":"Definitions Governance owner"}],
  "responses": [{"concept_id":"concept:term","action":"propose","payload":{"definition":"Candidate meaning."}}]
}
```

The advanced path supports `reuse`, `specialize`, `propose`, `open`, `defer`, and `refuse`.
Open dispositions cause exit code `4`; they never invent an answer.

Exit codes: `0` complete candidate pack or compiled handoff, `2` CLI/input error,
`3` context, compiler, or structural failure, and `4` open meaning or a handoff
readiness block. All outputs retain `authority_effect: none`.

# CyberAlchemy v2 Capability Ontology

Status: canonical shared ontology package
Visibility: private
Owner: CyberAlchemy v2 capability owner
Ontology type: `business-system-bridge`
Canonical definitions: `CAV2-D67` Product Capability and public
`DEF-ARC-CAPABILITY` Agent Capability

## Why this package exists

CyberAlchemy already describes several things as capabilities, but those records
use different local shapes. Without a shared ontology, “capability” can mean a
product outcome, an agent behavior, a component, a command, a permission, or a
passing run. Those meanings are not interchangeable.

This package makes the distinction explicit:

- a **Product Capability** says what useful outcome CyberAlchemy must enable;
- an **Agent Capability** says what reusable work an agent can perform under an
  owned contract;
- a **Capability Realization** is an agent or system mechanism that may realize
  part of a Product Capability;
- a **Capability Reference** points to a source-owned capability without taking
  ownership of it.

# Define Capability

Status: perennial candidate. No authority effect.
Owner: CyberAlchemy v2 product owner.

In plain terms: this is a long-lived proposal. It grants no permission to act.

## Purpose

Work depends on more than a task description. People also need to know:

- what result is wanted;
- why it matters;
- where the work applies;
- which terms and ideas must be understood;
- where current information came from;
- who may decide unclear points; and
- which questions are still open.

Define collects those answers before work starts and while it continues. When an
answer is missing, Define uses visible, provenance-bearing work context before
asking the person to repeat it. If that context is still insufficient or
indeterminate, Define records and asks the question instead of guessing.

## Goal And Intent

A **goal** is the specific result wanted, including its limits.

An **intent** is the original reason for that goal. It records the problem,
purpose, and desired change.

Example:

- Goal: a customer can request a refund.
- Intent: reduce manual support work without refunding the wrong person.

Define may clarify the wording, but it must keep the goal linked to the original
intent.

## Definition

A **concept** is an important term or idea that the work depends on. **Context**
says where that concept is being used, such as one feature, domain, user group,
or time period.

A **source** is the exact place information came from. **Evidence** is
information used to support a statement or decision. A **relationship** is a
named link between two concepts. An **owner** is the person or role allowed to
decide one exact matter.

CyberAlchemy Define is a capability with stated owners and permission limits. It:

1. keeps the goal and intent visible;
2. lists the concepts needed for this context;
3. finds existing definitions, sources, evidence, relationships, and owners;
4. asks a question when a concept is missing, unclear, or disputed;
5. records one current handling choice for every required concept; and
6. produces a checked bundle for the next person, team, or tool.

That handling choice is called a **disposition**:

- reuse;
- specialize;
- propose; or
- open.

The checked bundle is called a **Definition Pack**.

## Handled Definition Registry

Define keeps context-bound definition handling records in a separate candidate
registry. A record identifies the concept and context, states one current
disposition—reuse, specialize, propose, or open—and retains its exact sources,
decision owner, consumers, and challenge or refresh route.

The registry is not the canonical definition store. Its product owner owns the
registry asset, Definitions Governance stewards the record contract, source and
decision owners retain authority over meaning, and a later runtime may only
persist records under a separately accepted implementation contract. The
initial registry is empty because no real bounded Define context has yet
produced a handled record in this package.

## Why Define Exists

Teams lose time when:

- the same word has different meanings in different files;
- a correct definition is used outside its intended context;
- the reason for a choice is lost;
- nobody knows who may answer a question; or
- a question disappears between tools or sessions.

Define keeps each concept linked to its context, source, owner, and open
questions.

This capability definition already has evidence behind it. It reuses 10 active
CAV2 definitions, the CAV2 product thesis and product ontology, existing Arcanum
Define and Invoke mechanics, and the DomainSpec v2 Define CLI model. The current
validation receipt also shows that the package remains linked to the exact
recorded source bytes.

That evidence supports the problem, capability shape, method, authority limits,
and feasibility. We still need measured use evidence to know how much the
finished product reduces repeated explanations, hidden disagreements, or user
effort.

## Inputs

Define needs:

- a goal with stated limits;
- the intent behind the goal;
- the context where the result will be used;
- the person, team, or tool that needs the result;
- available documents, records, and other evidence;
- known owners; and
- existing questions or constraints.

Missing context follows the ordered resolution contract below. Any other missing
input becomes an open question.

## Context Resolution And Sufficiency

Define resolves the context needed for the stated job in a fixed order:

1. use intent context and related references explicitly supplied by the user;
2. if needed, derive candidate context from the current context window;
3. if still needed, derive candidate context from the current saved Define
   Session; and
4. if the bounded context is still insufficient or indeterminate, ask whether
   the user wants to provide more context.

Each derived item remains candidate context. Define records its source kind,
source reference or session revision, derivation posture, confidence, and any
conflict with explicit user context. Explicit user context always outranks a
machine-derived candidate, and the user may correct, reject, or replace any
candidate.

A semantic sufficiency evaluation is made against the needs of the current
Define job, not against an impossible standard of complete human intent. It
returns exactly one status:

- `sufficient` — the stated job can continue with the recorded bounded context;
- `insufficient` — named required context is missing; or
- `indeterminate` — the available evidence cannot support either conclusion.

Only `sufficient` satisfies the context prerequisite. The other states preserve
the missing or disputed context and create a visible invitation for more context.
Silence is not an answer. Inference, confidence, evaluator output, or a receipt
does not create user intent, ownership, approval, or authority.

The existing private semantic-judgment evaluator is a bounded feasibility
witness for deterministic reduction, provenance, residue, and insufficiency. It
is not yet the Define-specific evaluator described here and does not prove this
flow is implemented.

## Work

Define performs these steps:

1. resolve and evaluate the bounded context using the ordered source ladder;
2. list the concepts needed to understand the goal in that context;
3. search owned sources before creating a new definition;
4. check where each definition applies and who owns it;
5. record conflicting uses instead of silently choosing one;
6. ask one useful question when an important gap remains;
7. give every required concept one current disposition; and
8. check that sources, owners, relationships, context provenance, sufficiency,
   and open questions are visible.

## Result

The result is a [Definition Pack](DEFINITION-PACK.md). It keeps these items
together:

- goal, intent, and context;
- required concepts and dispositions;
- definitions and exact sources;
- evidence and relationships;
- owners;
- open questions;
- check results; and
- permission limits.

The next team may use the pack, challenge it, or send new questions back to
Define.

## Boundaries

Define clarifies concepts and context. It does not choose:

- product behavior;
- system architecture;
- UX flow or UI form;
- brand expression;
- implementation tasks;
- execution, publication, or deployment; or
- formally accepting a definition into the canonical definition store.

Define is not a mandatory stage before every design task. Use it when unclear
concepts or missing context would cause guessing, rework, or an ownership
conflict.

## Example

Example only: this does not define “customer” or authorize implementation.

A product team wants to add refunds.

    Goal: A customer can request a refund.
    Intent: Reduce manual support work without refunding the wrong person.
    Context: Refund eligibility for the online shop.

The concept “customer” is unclear. It could mean the buyer, account owner, or
gift recipient.

Define checks current sources and asks:

> Which owned definition applies to this refund context, and who may decide?

The current disposition may be reuse, specialize, propose, or open. Define
records the choice, source, owner, and remaining question. It does not design the
refund screen or choose the payment API.

## Owners

- The **goal owner** owns the goal and its original intent.
- A **source owner** owns meaning inside that source's stated context.
- The **CyberAlchemy v2 product owner** owns the candidate product meaning of
  Define.
- The **Definitions Governance owner** decides whether a definition candidate
  enters the canonical definition store.
- The **owner of the next use** decides whether the pack is suitable input for
  that use.

## Claim Ceiling

This candidate capability is supported by reused definitions, prior product and
ontology work, existing mechanics, runtime modeling, and source validation.
That evidence does not by itself establish measured customer outcomes, complete
understanding, a finished CyberAlchemy runtime, ease of use, canonical artifact
admission, definition promotion, or permission to execute downstream work.

# Define Lifecycles

Status: perennial candidate. No authority effect.
Owners: CyberAlchemy v2 product owner and CyberAlchemy v2 Define runtime owner.

In plain terms: this is a long-lived proposal. It grants no permission to act.
The product owner controls the proposed capability meaning. The runtime owner
controls the software contract.

## Purpose

A **lifecycle** is an ordered set of states. It shows where something is now,
what may happen next, who decides, and what each state proves.

Define has two separate lifecycles:

1. the lifecycle of the Define package and its documents; and
2. the lifecycle of one saved Define session.

Keeping them separate matters. A completed session does not approve the package,
promote a definition, or accept a runtime.

## Handled Definition Record Lifecycle

A handled-definition record belongs to one explicit concept, context, and
intended use. It begins as one of four dispositions: reuse, specialize, propose,
or open. A later material change creates a successor record; it does not rewrite
the earlier source state. At most one record for the same concept and context is
current.

Reuse must retain the exact canonical source state. Specialize and propose remain
candidates with all required definition voices and boundaries. Open retains the
question, affected use, stop decision, and next action without inventing a
normative definition. Supersession, validation, or registry presence does not
promote a record or implement persistence.

## Product Asset Lifecycle

The **product asset** is this Define package: its documents, machine-readable
records, schema, validator, and receipts.

In this lifecycle:

- **promoted** means formally accepted into the canonical definition store;
- **runtime adopted** means the runtime owner accepted one exact software
  contract; and
- **runtime rebound** means current capability records identify the standalone
  Define runtime without implying conformance or adoption.

It moves through these states:

    source evidence pinned
      -> candidate package authored
      -> candidate package validated
      -> product owner reviewed
      -> definitions promoted by a separate decision
      -> runtime adopted by a separate decision
      -> runtime rebound to exact candidate bytes

| State | Concrete result | Owner | What is still not proved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source evidence pinned | Exact source files, versions, and text locations are recorded. | Define package author | The product meaning is correct. |
| Candidate package authored | A private proposal exists as a complete file set. | CyberAlchemy v2 product owner | The proposal is canonical or implemented. |
| Candidate package validated | Required files, fields, links, and current sources pass their checks. | Independent package validator | The proposal is correct, valuable, or approved. |
| Product owner reviewed | The product owner accepts one exact proposal for further review. | CyberAlchemy v2 product owner | Definitions are canonical or implementation may start. |
| Definitions promoted | Exact definition candidates enter the canonical definition store. | Definitions Governance owner | A runtime is accepted. |
| Runtime rebound | Current capability records identify one exact standalone runtime. | Define capability owner | Behavioral conformance or adoption is proved. |
| Runtime adopted | One exact runtime contract is accepted. | Define runtime owner | Anything is published, released, or deployed. |

The current package state is **candidate package validated**. Its PASS receipt
says the files are complete, connected, structurally valid, and current against
their recorded sources. Candidate means the package has not crossed the later
owner review and promotion steps; it does not mean the package lacks evidence.

## Define Session Lifecycle

A **Define Session** is the saved record for one goal. It keeps the goal, intent,
context, concepts, questions, answers, sources, owners, and handling choices
together. Those handling choices are called dispositions: reuse, specialize,
propose, or open.

The proposed session states are:

    created
      -> goal, intent, and context recorded
      -> sources and required concepts found
      -> questions opened, answered, deferred, or routed
      -> one disposition recorded for each concept
      -> Definition Pack checked
      -> pack handed to the named person, team, or tool
      -> session refreshed or closed

Creating a session only gives it an ID. It does not show that any concept is
correct or accepted.

The CyberAlchemy runtime does not implement this full lifecycle yet.

## Stop Conditions

Define stops and asks for an owner decision when:

- the goal, intent, or context is disputed;
- two owners give incompatible meanings for the same context;
- a proposed disposition would overwrite canonical meaning;
- a question would change product meaning, who may decide, or what effect is
  allowed;
- the next action would pass the recorded permission limit; or
- required evidence cannot be found and the next use cannot accept that gap.

Stopping is not failure. The session keeps the question, reason, owner, and next
step visible.

## Example

Example only: this does not define “customer,” appoint a real billing-domain
owner, or authorize implementation.

One refund session may move through these states:

    created
      -> goal recorded: “customer can request a refund”
      -> intent recorded: “reduce support work safely”
      -> context recorded: “online-shop refund eligibility”
      -> “customer” found to be unclear
      -> question routed to a suggested billing-domain owner
      -> gift-recipient refund remains open
      -> pack checked and sent to product and engineering

This may close one Define session. It does not make “customer” a canonical
CyberAlchemy definition. Definitions Governance must decide that separately.

## Claim Ceiling

These lifecycle descriptions do not prove an implemented state machine, saved
runtime state, CLI and chat synchronization, definition promotion, runtime
adoption, or any external package migration.
